input: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures in order to characterise the temperature sensitivity of the reaction. At 300 K, the value of k was found to be 0.08 s-1. At the higher temperature of 340 K, the value of k was 4.206 s-1, this figure having been computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 84 kJ mol-1, and it is presented as a derived value rather than as a direct experimental measurement. Each temperature was investigated in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which gives an indication of the reproducibility of the measurements. It should be noted that no rate constant is reported above 340 K, because at temperatures above 340 K the solvent was found to evaporate during the sampling process, which meant that reliable measurements could no longer be obtained under those conditions. The results nevertheless provide a clear indication of the strong temperature dependence exhibited by this particular reaction system over the range studied. The investigation forms part of a wider programme of work on the reaction, in which the temperature dependence of the rate is required for the design of the reactor in which the reaction is to be carried out on a larger scale.
target: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, each measurement in triplicate. At 300 K, k = 0.08 s-1. At 340 K, k = 4.206 s-1. The 340 K value is a derived value: it was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 84 kJ mol-1, and it is reported as computed, not as a direct measurement. The relative standard deviation of k across the replicate measurements was 4%. No rate constant is reported above 340 K: above that temperature the solvent evaporated during sampling, so samples taken there did not hold the composition they were drawn at, and no value from them is stated. The two values as reported therefore rest on different footings: the lower-temperature value is a measurement with its stated spread, and the higher-temperature value is a calculation from the stated activation energy, carrying the standing of the relation and of the activation energy rather than of a further set of replicates. The activation energy is the same quantity that links the two temperatures in the Arrhenius relation, and the computed value inherits any error in it directly. A reader who needs the rate constant between the two temperatures obtains it from the same relation and the same activation energy, on the same footing as the computed value.
